known_differences: A named escape \N{...} is not decoded: the document has unavailable text. CPython decodes it.
A lone surrogate escape gives unavailable text. CPython stores the surrogate.

A literal with a carriage return byte in its interior (CRLF, a lone CR, or a backslash before CR) has pending text and one pending assessment. CPython normalizes line endings before it reads the literal.
U+001C to U+001F are not stripped as whitespace by the cleanup. inspect.cleandoc strips them.

A literal that CPython rejects is still a document where the pinned grammar gives a string node: a short \x escape gives unavailable text, and a literal with a long run of prefix letters is read as a raw literal.

The string of a statement like (1 . "b"), which the grammar recovers with an ERROR inside the parentheses, gives nothing in the source view. The legacy role row still answers Docstring for it, and the legacy LOC view credits no documentation row. The three views differed on this shape before this unit, which changes neither legacy answer.

named_limitations.name: an excluded range directly after a value
named_limitations.detail: In a parse with excluded ranges, the position check covers the bytes before a docstring and the bytes of its value, not the bytes after the value up to the end of its statement. A statement that is longer in the full source, such as "doc" .upper() with the call excluded, is read as a docstring of the module, and its association is resolved. A definition whose body ends in the excluded gap is also a resolved owner; a definition whose body continues after the gap is pending.
named_limitations.reference: CPython reads the full source: no docstring.

pending: Binding owners and attribute documents: a string run after an assignment gives one pending assessment and no document
